video_metadata.working_title: WASHINGTON 1982 Cold Case Solved After 19 Years — Justice for the Green River Victims
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: Between 1982 and the mid-1980s dozens of girls and young women vanished from the Pacific Highway South strip near Sea-Tac Airport in King County, Washington; a task force that rose to dozens of detectives and then shrank to one man kept the case alive until 2001, when a saliva sample taken from truck painter Gary Leon Ridgway in 1987 was matched by improved DNA testing, leading to his 2003 guilty plea to 48 murders (49 in 2011) and to identifications of the last known unnamed victims as late as 2024.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: Grief and dignity for the victims, frustration at the lost years, and respect for the families and detectives who refused to let the names be forgotten.
video_metadata.research_method_note: Research done on 2026-10-11. Page fetching was blocked by the network proxy, so facts come from web-search result summaries (15 queries, shared budget) cross-checked with well-documented public background. Every timeline event and quote carries a source number matching the numbered source list in investigacion.md. Items marked BACKGROUND are widely documented but were not directly confirmed in a search snippet this session; items marked UNCERTAIN are flagged in notes_and_gaps and are not used as hard claims in the script.

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Gary Leon Ridgway (convicted). The story is centred on the victims; Ridgway is introduced late as the convicted offender.
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: 33 in the summer of 1982 (born February 18, 1949, BACKGROUND); 52 at his arrest on November 30, 2001; 54 at his guilty plea on November 5, 2003; 77 in October 2026.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Truck painter at the Kenworth truck plant in Renton, Washington, where he had worked since 1969 (AP via HeraldNet [7]). Now serving life without parole at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla [23][24].
protagonist.location: South King County, Washington: the area around Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, Pacific Highway South, Kent, Auburn, Des Moines, Renton.
protagonist.physical_description: Not used in script beyond archival photos.
protagonist.background_brief: Worked at Kenworth in Renton from 1969 until his 2001 arrest [7]. Came to investigators' attention in 1983 after the disappearance of Marie Malvar [26]; interviewed by King County detective Randy Mullinax in the mid-1980s and passed a polygraph in 1984 [27]; his home and vehicles were searched in April 1987 and he gave a saliva sample by chewing on gauze [5][6].
protagonist.psychological_profile: Not speculated. Judge Richard Jones described his 'Teflon-coated emotions and complete absence of compassion' at sentencing [12][14].
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: Not used: the channel does not humanize the offender. The documented twist is ordinariness: a long-time factory painter who clocked in at the same plant for three decades [7].
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: 'The Green River Killer' (media name, after the river where the first victims were found).

victims_or_targets._instructions: People affected by the protagonist's actions. Include 3-5 key figures minimum.

individuals.name: Wendy Lee Coffield
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Count in the 2003 plea; charged March 2003 on paint-sphere evidence [30][31]
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Last seen in Tacoma July 8, 1982; found in the Green River near Kent July 15, 1982 [2]
individuals.humanizing_detail: The first victim found; for years her name opened every list of the case [1][2]

individuals.name: Debra Lynn Bonner
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Disappeared July 25, 1982; found in the Green River August 12, 1982 [3][4]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her discovery is the date local media mark as the opening of the case [3]

individuals.name: Marcia Faye Chapman
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Disappeared August 1, 1982, near the airport strip; found in the Green River August 15, 1982 [2][29]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Oldest of the three women found on August 15

individuals.name: Cynthia Jean Hinds
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Charged December 2001; tied by circumstantial evidence per AP [7] (Oxygen [5] lists her among DNA matches: conflict noted)
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Disappeared August 11, 1982; found in the Green River near Kent August 15, 1982 [2][29]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Found in the water beside Marcia Chapman [29]

individuals.name: Opal Charmaine Mills
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Last seen August 12, 1982, at a phone booth off the strip; found on the riverbank August 15, 1982 [2][29]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Last seen at a phone booth: in 1982, a phone booth was how a teenager called home [2]

individuals.name: Carol Ann Christensen
individuals.role_or_profession: Young mother of a five-year-old daughter, Sarah
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her daughter Sarah King was five when she died [13]

individuals.name: Linda Jane Rule
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her father Robert Rule forgave the killer in court [10]

individuals.name: Marie Malvar
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Plea count; her disappearance first linked Ridgway's truck to the case [26]
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Disappeared April 30, 1983, after getting into a pickup; her boyfriend followed it [26]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her family and boyfriend searched for the truck themselves [26]

individuals.name: Debra Lorraine Estes
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her mother Carol Estes spoke at sentencing [13]

individuals.name: Rebecca 'Becky' Marrero
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Disappeared December 1982; remains found in Auburn in December 2010 (BACKGROUND)
individuals.humanizing_detail: Missing 28 years before she was found

individuals.name: Lori Anne Razpotnik
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Plea count as an unidentified victim ('Bones 17') [21][22]
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Ran away from her Lewis County home in 1982; remains found in Auburn December 30, 1985; identified December 2023 [21][22]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her mother's saliva sample confirmed her name 38 years later [21]

individuals.name: Tammie Liles
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Partial remains found near Tigard, Oregon, in 1985 and identified by dental records in 1988; a second set ('Bones 20') found in south King County after Ridgway led investigators there in 2003; identified January 22, 2024 [19][20]
individuals.humanizing_detail: Her mother gave the DNA that confirmed the match [20]

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Girls and young women, many of them teenagers and runaways, most of them last seen on or near Pacific Highway South (the 'Sea-Tac Strip') between 1982 and 1984 [1][2]
collective_victims_if_applicable.total_number_affected: 49 convictions (48 in 2003, 1 in 2011) [11][17]; Ridgway claimed as many as 71 [1-summary][39]
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Murdered; several left unidentified for decades as 'Bones' numbers; families waited up to 41 years for a name [19][21]

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Dave Reichert
characters.role_in_story: King County detective, one of the first at the August 15, 1982 scene [28][29]; later elected King County Sheriff in 1997 and reassembled the Green River detectives [34]; later a member of Congress (BACKGROUND)
characters.key_actions_they_took: Led the early investigation; as sheriff called detectives back to the case including Tom Jensen [34]; in April 2024 talked to Kent students about the case [28]

characters.name: Tom Jensen
characters.role_in_story: King County detective; the sole full-time investigator on the Green River case in the early 1990s [36][35]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Volunteered to stay on the case when the task force was disbanded in 1990 [35]; was among the detectives called back in 1997 [34]
characters.notable_quotes: His son Jeff Jensen wrote: 'One detective was to continue working Green River full time. My father volunteered for the job.' [35]

characters.name: Major Richard Kraske
characters.role_in_story: Head of the Criminal Investigation Division; formed the first task force in 1982 [29][33]

characters.name: Captain Frank Adamson
characters.role_in_story: Commander of the reorganized Green River Task Force from January 1984 to 1986 [33][36]

characters.name: Randy Mullinax
characters.role_in_story: King County detective who interviewed Ridgway in the mid-1980s [27]

characters.name: Beverly Himick
characters.role_in_story: Washington State Patrol Crime Laboratory forensic scientist [5]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Re-examined preserved evidence in 2001 and developed the profiles compared to the 1987 sample [5]

characters.name: Microtrace laboratory (Skip Palenik, BACKGROUND for the name)
characters.key_actions_they_took: In March 2003 matched microscopic paint spheres on victims' clothing to paint used at Kenworth [31]

characters.name: Norm Maleng
characters.key_actions_they_took: Filed the 2001 charges; agreed to the 2003 plea deal sparing the death penalty in exchange for confession and help locating remains [18]
characters.notable_quotes: 'When I made the decision, I felt at peace with it. I did then, and I do today.' [18]

characters.name: Judge Richard Jones
characters.key_actions_they_took: Ordered 48 seconds of silence; imposed 48 consecutive life terms and a $480,000 fine [12][13]
characters.notable_quotes: Spoke of 'the final chapter of your reign of terror in our community' and Ridgway's 'Teflon-coated emotions and complete absence of compassion' [12][14]

characters.name: Robert Rule
characters.role_in_story: Father of Linda Rule, from Everett [10]
characters.key_actions_they_took: Forgave Ridgway in court; the only moment Ridgway broke down [10]
characters.notable_quotes: 'Mr. Ridgway, there are people here that hate you. I'm not one of them. I forgive you for what you have done.' [13]

characters.name: Sarah King
characters.notable_quotes: 'I was only five when my mother died and my dad told me I would never see her again.' / 'No matter what you say, I will never, ever, ever forgive you.' [13]

characters.name: Robert (Bobby) Woods
characters.key_actions_they_took: Followed the pickup on April 30, 1983; with Marie's family later led police to Ridgway's truck [26]

characters.name: Carol Estes, Joan Mackie, Tim Meehan
characters.role_in_story: Mother of Debra Estes; mother of Cindy Smith; brother of Mary Meehan [13][12]

characters.name: Melvyn Foster
characters.role_in_story: Taxi driver publicly treated as a suspect in 1982; never charged (name BACKGROUND; article [38] reports a former suspect's sense of vindication)

chronological_timeline._instructions: List every significant event with exact dates when possible. This is the backbone of your script.

events.what_happened: Ridgway begins working as a truck painter at the Kenworth plant
events.significance: Same employer for 32 years; paint later becomes evidence

events.what_happened: Wendy Lee Coffield, 16, last seen
Wendy Coffield found in the river
Debra Lynn Bonner, 23, disappears

events.location: Pacific Highway South near the airport
events.what_happened: Marcia Faye Chapman, 31, disappears
Cynthia Jean Hinds, 17, disappears

events.location: Phone booth off the strip / Green River
events.what_happened: Opal Mills, 16, last seen at a phone booth; same day Debra Bonner is found in the river
Chapman and Hinds found in shallow water, Mills on the bank; Detective Dave Reichert among the first at the scene
events.significance: Five victims in a month: police recognize a serial killer

events.what_happened: King County Sheriff's Office sets up the Green River Task Force, 25 officers under Major Richard Kraske
First task force wound down by year's end
Lori Anne Razpotnik, 15, runs away from home
Linda Jane Rule, 16, killed
Marie Malvar, 18, gets into a pickup; boyfriend Robert Woods follows and loses it at a light
events.significance: Family and boyfriend later lead police to Ridgway's truck

events.what_happened: Carol Christensen found
Task force reorganized under Captain Frank Adamson
Ridgway interviewed by detective Randy Mullinax and passes a polygraph
Partial remains later identified (1988, dental) as Tammie Liles found
City of Auburn workers find remains later known as Bones 16 and Bones 17
Search warrant on home and vehicles; nothing to justify arrest; Ridgway chews on gauze to give a saliva sample
events.significance: The sample that solves the case 14 years later

events.what_happened: Sheriff's Department disbands the task force; one detective, Tom Jensen, stays on full time
Dave Reichert elected King County Sheriff; calls detectives back to the case including Jensen
Forensic scientist Beverly Himick re-examines preserved evidence; profiles from three early victims match the 1987 saliva sample
Ridgway arrested as he leaves his shift
Prosecutor Norm Maleng charges four counts of aggravated first-degree murder: Chapman, Hinds, Mills, Christensen
events.significance: Date varies by source (AP Dec 4, KOMO Dec 5)

events.what_happened: Ridgway pleads not guilty
Three more counts filed for Coffield, Estes and Bonner after Microtrace matches microscopic paint spheres to Kenworth paint
Under the plea agreement Ridgway leads investigators to remains, including a second set of Tammie Liles's remains
Ridgway pleads guilty to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder in exchange for being spared the death penalty
events.significance: Largest number of convictions of any US serial killer at the time (BACKGROUND)

events.what_happened: Families speak; Robert Rule forgives; Judge Jones orders 48 seconds of silence and imposes 48 consecutive life terms and a $480,000 fine
Ridgway charged with and pleads guilty to the murder of Rebecca 'Becky' Marrero, his 49th conviction, under the 2003 agreement
DNA identifies Bones 16 as Sandra Majors
Washington formally abolishes the death penalty
Bones 17 identified as Lori Anne Razpotnik, 15, via Parabon NanoLabs genetic genealogy; confirmed with her mother's saliva by the University of North Texas
Sheriff's Office announces Bones 20 identified as Tammie Liles, 16, via Othram; no other unidentified remains believed connected to Ridgway
Ridgway temporarily transferred to King County to help search for undiscovered remains, then returned; cases remain open

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.exact_location: Green River near Kent, King County, Washington
the_moment.what_is_happening: Three more victims are found in and beside the river; a young King County detective, Dave Reichert, is among the first to arrive
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: Five girls and women found in one month; three of them teenagers
the_moment.ironic_twist: The man responsible gave police a saliva sample in 1987 that sat in storage until 2001; he painted trucks at the same plant the whole time.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: How could someone take dozens of girls and young women from one highway for years and stay free for nearly two decades?

the_method._instructions: How was the case solved? Technical details explained for a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: STR DNA re-testing of preserved evidence against a 1987 reference sample; microscopic paint-sphere trace analysis
step_by_step_explanation: 1987: saliva on gauze collected and kept [5]
1980s methods could not produce a usable profile from the small, old biological traces (BACKGROUND)
2001: WSP crime lab re-examines evidence from three early victims; newer methods build profiles [5][9]
Profiles compared to the 1987 sample: match [5][7]
2003: Microtrace links microscopic paint spheres on Coffield's and Estes's clothing to the specialized paint used at Kenworth [31]
the_method.why_it_worked: The evidence and the reference sample had been preserved for 14 to 19 years until the science caught up [5]

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: a genetic barcode read at a set of places in the DNA
a known sample from a known person to compare against
particles too small to see that move from a place or a person onto clothing

the_method.scale_of_operation: Evidence from 1982 compared against a 1987 sample in 2001

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Law enforcement and society's attitude toward the victims; budget and political pressure on the task force [33]
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Investigate every disappearance with equal urgency
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: Staff cuts and shifting politics [33][35]; limited forensic science in the 1980s [5]; a suspect who passed a polygraph [27]
specific_incompetence_examples: Ridgway's truck linked to Marie Malvar's disappearance in 1983 by her own family and boyfriend [26]
1987 saliva sample left untested in a usable way for 14 years [5]
Task force disbanded in 1990, leaving one detective [35]
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The answer was in police storage from April 1987 onward [5].

the_investigation.investigating_agency: King County Sheriff's Office Green River Task Force; Washington State Patrol Crime Laboratory; King County Prosecuting Attorney
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: A taxi driver was publicly treated as a suspect in 1982 and never charged [38] (name BACKGROUND)
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: 2001 DNA match to the 1987 saliva sample [5][7]
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Biological evidence left on early victims, preserved for 19 years [5]
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: About 19 years and 4 months from the first discovery (July 15, 1982 to November 30, 2001)

the_confrontation.date_and_time: November 30, 2001, as he left his shift [7]
the_confrontation.scene_description: Arrested by King County detectives at his workplace of 32 years [7]
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: He was arrested at the plant where he had painted trucks since 1969; paint from that plant later became evidence [7][31]

charges_filed: Dec 2001: 4 counts aggravated first-degree murder (Chapman, Hinds, Mills, Christensen) [7][8]
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: Families spoke at the December 18, 2003 sentencing; about 20 families, 10 minutes each [13]

legal_resolution.sentence_received: 48 consecutive life sentences without parole and a $480,000 fine (December 18, 2003) [12][13]; a 49th life sentence in 2011 [17]

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: The victims were dismissed by many at the time because of their age, poverty or circumstances; the case shows what happens when a society decides some missing girls matter less.
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Many victims were teenagers who had run away; any family can lose a child to the street for a season.
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Preserve evidence, never close the file, and treat every missing girl as someone's daughter.
universal_stakes.current_relevance: Genetic genealogy named the last unknown victims in 2023 and 2024; the cases remain open [19][21][24]

unverified_claims: Which three victims were DNA matches: AP [7] says Chapman, Mills, Christensen with Hinds circumstantial; Oxygen [5] says Mills, Chapman, Hinds with Christensen circumstantial. Script follows AP wording only loosely ('three of the four').
Charges date Dec 4 (AP) vs Dec 5 (KOMO, Oxygen) 2001.
Mullinax interview year: 1984 per summary of [27]; article headline implies 1985. Script says 'in the mid-1980s' and polygraph 'in 1984'.
Rafter discovery on August 15 [29]: date link single-sourced; script says only that a man on a raft saw bodies in the river.
Ridgway birth date, Navy service, ages of Estes and Marrero, Marrero remains found December 2010: BACKGROUND.
Melvyn Foster's name as the early suspect in [38]: BACKGROUND; script does not name him.
Claim of up to 71 victims comes from Ridgway himself; unverified.
The 'I killed so many women' line could not be confirmed and is not used.
